clinicalPearls: Anti-Ma2 (anti-Ta) targets the Ma2/PNMA2 protein expressed in neurons and testicular tissue.

In young men it is characteristically associated with testicular germ cell tumours; when antibodies to both Ma1 and Ma2 are present, older patients with lung, breast or other carcinomas are more typical.
The syndrome produces limbic, diencephalic and upper brainstem encephalitis, often in combination.
Diencephalic and hypothalamic involvement causes excessive daytime sleepiness, narcolepsy-like features with cataplexy, hyperphagia and endocrine disturbance.
Brainstem involvement may produce a vertical supranuclear gaze palsy that mimics progressive supranuclear palsy.
MRI frequently shows signal change in the medial temporal lobes, hypothalamus, thalamus and midbrain, sometimes with contrast enhancement.
When testicular imaging is normal but suspicion is high, biopsy or orchidectomy may be needed to detect intratubular germ cell neoplasia.
Compared with other onconeural antibody syndromes, younger men with a treated testicular tumour have a relatively better chance of neurological improvement.
reference.pathophysiology: Ma2 (PNMA2) is a protein normally restricted to neurons and the testis. Germ cell tumours of the testis, or other carcinomas that aberrantly express Ma proteins, provoke an onconeural immune response in which the antibody acts as a diagnostic marker while antigen-specific T-cell mechanisms are thought to mediate neuronal injury. The disorder preferentially targets the limbic system, the diencephalon and hypothalamus, and the rostral brainstem, producing a characteristic tripartite encephalitis. Hypothalamic involvement disrupts orexin/hypocretin signalling and other regulatory pathways, generating hypersomnia, narcolepsy-cataplexy, hyperphagia and endocrine failure, while midbrain involvement affects vertical gaze pathways. Inflammatory infiltrates and neuronal loss underlie the deficits, and the association with germ cell tumour antigens accounts for the striking predilection for young men.
additionalDifferentials: Other autoimmune limbic encephalitides such as anti-LGI1, anti-NMDA receptor, anti-AMPA or anti-GABA-B
Herpes simplex and other infective encephalitis
Progressive supranuclear palsy, given the vertical gaze palsy
Wernicke encephalopathy and other diencephalic lesions
Neurosarcoidosis or central nervous system lymphoma involving the diencephalon
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid anti-Ma2 and anti-Ma1 testing with confirmatory assays
Scrotal ultrasound in men, with consideration of biopsy or orchidectomy when imaging is normal but suspicion is high
Whole-body FDG-PET and CT to detect extragonadal or non-testicular tumours
MRI of the brain focusing on the medial temporal lobes, hypothalamus, thalamus and midbrain
Cerebrospinal fluid for lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein and oligoclonal bands
Serum tumour markers such as alpha-fetoprotein and beta-hCG for germ cell tumours
Endocrine and hypothalamic-pituitary axis testing, with sleep studies and cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin where narcolepsy is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive encephalitis with reduced consciousness
Vertical gaze palsy and brainstem signs threatening bulbar function
Occult testicular or germ cell tumour requiring urgent evaluation, including orchidectomy when indicated
Severe hypersomnia or cataplexy causing injury
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is more favourable than in anti-Hu or anti-Yo disease, particularly in younger men whose testicular tumour is identified and treated early, when neurological stabilisation or improvement can occur. Older patients with combined Ma1/Ma2 reactivity and extratesticular tumours generally fare worse.
pitfalls: Diagnosing idiopathic narcolepsy and missing the paraneoplastic cause
Mistaking the vertical gaze palsy for progressive supranuclear palsy
Concluding the testes are tumour-free on ultrasound alone without considering biopsy or orchidectomy
Failing to distinguish isolated Ma2 from combined Ma1/Ma2 reactivity, which alters the tumour search and prognosis
Attributing hypersomnia and hyperphagia to psychiatric or metabolic causes
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Consensus diagnostic criteria for paraneoplastic neurological syndromes
management: Identify and treat the underlying tumour — orchidectomy for a testicular germ cell tumour in young men, or treatment of the relevant carcinoma when combined Ma1/Ma2 reactivity indicates extratesticular disease
Immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, escalating in resistant disease
Symptomatic treatment of narcolepsy-cataplexy and excessive daytime sleepiness with wakefulness-promoting agents
Hormone replacement for hypothalamic-pituitary endocrine failure and management of hyperphagia
Persistent search for an occult germ cell tumour with repeat scrotal imaging and consideration of orchidectomy when suspicion remains high despite normal imaging
Multidisciplinary neurology, oncology and endocrinology follow-up with tumour surveillance
